qs.q: Which laboratory finding is characteristic of a patient with hyperglycemia caused by an insulinoma rather than exogenous insulin administration?
o: C. Low insulin and high C-peptide
B. High insulin and low C-peptide
D. Low insulin and low C-peptide
A. High insulin and high C-peptide
qs.e: Insulin is secreted with equimolar amounts of C-peptide, meaning endogenous hyperinsulinism from an insulinoma results in high levels of both. Exogenous insulin administration leads to high insulin but low C-peptide levels.

Hypoglycaemic symptoms, documented low glucose level, and symptom relief after glucose intake.

Hypertension, headache, and palpitations occurring together.
qs.e: Most common pancreatic NET, 90% benign. Suppressed C-peptide during hypoglycaemia if exogenous insulin; elevated C-peptide in insulinoma.

ai.title: Insulinoma
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Insulinoma is a rare pancreatic β‑cell tumour that causes inappropriate insulin secretion, leading to recurrent hypoglycaemia. Diagnosis rests on Whipple's triad and supervised fasting, but limited resources require pragmatic alternatives.

sections.p: Insulinoma is the most common functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, usually benign and solitary, occurring in 1–4 per million people, often in the fourth decade.
b: Incidence peaks 30‑50 years; slight female predominance
Most are sporadic; 10 % linked to MEN1 syndrome
Tumour size <2 cm in >80 % of cases

sections.p: Normal β‑cells release insulin in response to rising plasma glucose, promoting peripheral glucose uptake and hepatic glycogen synthesis. Insulinoma cells lose glucose‑sensing control, secreting insulin continuously.
b: Insulin binds IR → PI3K‑Akt pathway → GLUT4 translocation
Result: ↑ peripheral glucose uptake, ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis
Loss of feedback → hypoglycaemia despite low glucose

sections.p: Physiologic insulin release is suppressed by low glucose, catecholamines, glucagon, and somatostatin. Insulinoma cells often lack functional K‑ATP channels, rendering them unresponsive to glucose‑mediated inhibition.
b: K‑ATP channel mutations (rare) mimic sulfonylurea effect
Somatostatin analogues can blunt secretion when needed

sections.p: Autonomous insulin secretion drives recurrent fasting hypoglycaemia, producing neuroglycopenic and autonomic symptoms.
b: Whipple's triad: symptoms, low plasma glucose, symptom relief after glucose

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, insulinoma may be mistaken for malaria, TB, or malnutrition‑related hypoglycaemia; careful history and bedside glucose testing are essential.
b: Typical presentation: fasting hypoglycaemia episodes, often nocturnal
Weight gain common due to frequent carbohydrate intake
Rarely, malignant insulinoma with metastases to liver or lymph nodes

t.b: Does the patient develop symptomatic hypoglycaemia with inappropriately high insulin? → Diagnosis if glucose <2.8 mmol/L, insulin ≥3 µU/mL, C‑peptide ≥0.2 nmol/L
Is the patient symptomatic with glucose <2.8 mmol/L? → Immediate treatment; supports suspicion when fasting test unavailable
High insulin with high C‑peptide rules out exogenous insulin use
Detects tumour >1 cm in tail or head; limited sensitivity
Localises tumour for surgery; preferred imaging

sections.p: Focus on pattern of hypoglycaemia, exclusion of surreptitious insulin, and localisation strategies suitable for resource‑limited environments.
b: Always confirm Whipple's triad before ordering costly imaging
In absence of fasting test, document at least two episodes with documented low glucose and symptom relief after glucose
When imaging unavailable, consider intra‑operative palpation of pancreas

whenToSeekHelp: Severe neuroglycopenic symptoms (seizure, loss of consciousness)

faq.q: Is MEN1 common in East Africa?
faq.a: MEN1 is rare worldwide; consider only if family history of pituitary or parathyroid tumours.

faq.q: What is the first emergency step?
faq.a: Give rapid IV glucose (50 % dextrose) and monitor consciousness.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with nocturnal tremor and confusion; capillary glucose 2.4 mmol/L. What is your next diagnostic step? — Perform a supervised fast if feasible; otherwise document a second episode with documented low glucose.
How does Whipple's triad differentiate insulinoma from malaria‑related hypoglycaemia? — Malaria may cause low glucose but not reproducible fasting hypoglycaemia with relief after glucose.
Why is C‑peptide measurement essential when insulinoma is suspected? — It distinguishes endogenous insulin secretion from exogenous insulin administration.
In a centre without CT, how would you localise an insulinoma? — Use high‑resolution abdominal ultrasound and, if surgery is planned, intra‑operative palpation of the pancreas.
What feature on history suggests a malignant insulinoma? — Rapid weight loss, persistent hypoglycaemia despite tumour resection, or imaging showing liver lesions.
Why are somatostatin analogues rarely first‑line for insulinoma? — They control symptoms but do not cure the tumour; surgery remains definitive.
A patient on sulfonylureas has hypoglycaemia; how do you rule out insulinoma? — Stop sulfonylurea, repeat fasting test; persistent inappropriate insulin points to tumour.
What urgent complication can arise from untreated insulinoma? — Recurrent severe hypoglycaemia leading to irreversible brain injury or death.
